item.title: Signs of Life and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Multicenter Observational Study
item.description:
Background: The prognostic value of individual signs of life (SOLs) remains unclear in patients experiencing traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (t-OHCA).

Objectives: To describe clinical outcomes among patients with t-OHCA by the presence of each SOL at the scene.

Methods: Data from the SOS-KANTO 2017 study, a multicenter prospective registry of OHCA cases treated between 2019 and 2021, were retrospectively analyzed. Adult patients diagnosed with t-OHCA were included, excluding those with a palpable pulse upon emergency medical service (EMS) arrival. Patients were categorized into eight subgroups based on the presence of three SOLs at the scene-the pupillary light reflex, spontaneous respiration, and cardiac electrical activity - and descriptive analyses were performed. The primary outcome was survival beyond the emergency department (ED).

Results: Of the 462 patients included in the analysis, two (0.4%) exhibited all three SOLs, and 18 (3.9%) exhibited two SOLs; in the latter group, two demonstrated cardiac activity and a pupillary reflex, and 16 had cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration. Among the 124 patients (26.8%) with only one SOL, 117 had cardiac activity, three showed a pupillary reflex, and four exhibited spontaneous respiration. No SOLs were observed in 318 patients (68.8%). Overall, 22 patients (4.8%) survived beyond the ED. The highest survival rate was observed in the subgroup with both cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration (4/16; 25%), followed by the subgroup with cardiac activity alone (10/117; 8.5%).

Conclusions: Among the t-OHCA patients, survival beyond the ED was observed more frequently in those with cardiac electrical activity at the scene.

Yamashita I, Yamamoto R, Suzuki M, Kitamura N, Tagami T, Yasunaga H

item.title: Efficacy of Inhaled Methoxyflurane for Acute Trauma Pain Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Background: Acute traumatic pain is common in emergency settings and inadequate analgesia can worsen physiological, psychological, and functional outcomes.

Study objectives: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy, onset of action, safety, and clinical practicality of inhaled methoxyflurane compared with control analgesic treatments for acute trauma-related pain.

Methods: Four databases were searched from inception through February 2026. Randomized controlled trials evaluating inhaled methoxyflurane for acute traumatic pain were eligible. Outcomes included visual analogue scale and numerical rating scale pain scores, rescue analgesia, time to first pain relief, and adverse events (AEs). Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and RevMan was used for quantitative synthesis.

Results: Seven studies involving 1585 participants were analyzed. Methoxyflurane significantly reduced the time to first pain relief compared with controls (mean difference -5.93 min, 95% confidence interval [CI] -6.86 to -5.00, p < 0.00001, I2 = 0%). Pain intensity also favored methoxyflurane at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min. Methoxyflurane also significantly reduced the need for rescue analgesia (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.18-0.90, p = 0.03). Overall AEs were comparable, but dizziness, drowsiness, and cough were more frequent with methoxyflurane.

Conclusion: Inhaled methoxyflurane provides rapid and effective analgesia for acute traumatic pain and may reduce rescue analgesia needs. Further high-quality randomized trials are needed to clarify comparative effectiveness across trauma populations and emergency care settings.

Husain AZ, Alsahli ASM, Alghamdi AMA, Mulla MI, Alotaibi SF, Alsaeed MA
